=== FILE: videos/2020-03-17_oR2S_GTatSQ_numbers-don-t-lie-using-data-in-the-weight-room-to-enhance-o/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: oR2S_GTatSQ
title: "SSAC20: Numbers Don't Lie: Using Data in the Weight Room to Enhance On-Field Performance"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Jeremy Jacobs]
topics: [american-football, sports-science]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

An LSU assistant strength and conditioning coach describes how his football program uses three data sources (camera-based bar velocity, force plates and GPS) to guide weekly lifting decisions. His argument is that load prescribed from a one-rep max ignores day-to-day nervous system state, whereas a velocity target adjusts to the athlete. He shows how force plate trends and practice GPS data help explain readiness dips, and claims the team's measures rose through the season, ending with its fastest practice speeds before the championship game. The talk is a single-program case study with no comparison group, so it supports a practical workflow more than a general result.

## Key claims

- A strength coach spends more time with athletes than anyone else on staff, which helps individualize training. [01:04]
- Football's fixed weekly schedule lets him plan performance week to week. [02:36]
- The program uses a camera system on every rack (22 racks), force plates and GPS units. [04:11]
- He is not interested in data that does not change what the program does, and he passes summaries to the head strength coach for programming decisions. [05:12]
- Velocity-based training lets him train the bar speed he wants rather than a fixed percentage of a tested max. [06:14]
- Newer cameras and cloud storage made velocity tracking usable every day, with data available at his desk after a session. [07:49]
- Football is a power sport, and strength gains that do not transfer to the field are questionable. [08:54]
- The aim is to move the force-velocity curve right (a heavier load moved faster), which he says correlates with field speed seen in GPS. [09:24]
- A falling eccentric braking number tells him to add strength work. [11:28]
- A tested one-rep max can swing day to day, so a fixed percentage may be too heavy or too light. [11:59]
- Everyone on the team can train at the same target velocity regardless of how they feel. [13:01]
- Accumulated data lets him build individual force-velocity profiles and set a starting load for a target velocity. [15:04]
- If the bar moves slower than expected at that load, he removes weight; if faster, he exploits the good day. [15:34]
- In season, peak power falls off at lower loads on squat, bench and deadlift than on Olympic lifts. [17:07]
- Some athletes set personal records mid-season because the velocity target was beaten before enough weight could slow them. [18:08]
- Load was adjusted by opponent (lighter and faster before the biggest game, harder before games expected to be won). [19:39]
- A dip in force plate data sends him back to bar percentages, bar velocities and practice GPS load. [20:11]
- Force plate measures rose weekly through the season, and the fastest practice GPS speeds came in the final week before the national championship game against Clemson. [20:41], [21:13]

## Numbers and definitions

- Racks with cameras: 22. [04:11]
- Force plate metrics (four): RSI modified (explained as how fast the athlete reaches peak jump height, from three jumps) [09:56]; concentric rate of power development divided by body mass [10:57]; eccentric braking rate of force development [10:57]; peak power divided by body mass [11:28]. The caption for the second metric is garbled ("rate of power development"); it may be concentric rate of force development.
- One-rep max fluctuation: 18 percent up or down per day, giving a 36 percent window. [11:59] Speaker's figure, no source given.
- Example target velocity: 0.8 m/s. [13:01]
- Example profile result: 62.5 percent of one-rep max for an athlete to reach 0.8 m/s. [15:04]
- Peak power drops between 60 and 65 percent on squat, bench and deadlift. [17:07]
- Peak power drops between 80 and 85 percent on Olympic lifts, depending on technique. [17:07]
- He says he has been at LSU five seasons. [01:34]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Perch camera velocity tracking (caption: "perch"), VALD force plates, Polar GPS and heart rate. [03:40], [04:11], [04:42]
- Velocity zones in place of percentage-only prescription; credited to Soviet origins and popularized in the US in the 1990s by Louie Simmons of Westside Barbell (caption spelling "Louise Simmons"). [07:18]
- Individual force-velocity profiles from accumulated in-season data. [15:04]
- Weekly charts of velocity, load, peak power and force plate metrics, color-coded by opponent. [16:37], [19:09]
- Head athletic trainer named as Jack Murphy (caption). [01:34]

## Limits and open questions

- Single program, single season, no comparison group. The upward trends and fast final-week GPS speeds are the speaker's reading, with no statistics shown.
- No sample sizes, no number of athletes, and no raw figures in the captions.
- The 18 percent fluctuation and the peak-power windows are the speaker's own claims with no cited source.
- Mixed signals on method: he says he no longer needs a "coach's eye" [21:13] but also modifies plans by hand for individual athletes and genetics [17:37].
- Lowering load before the biggest game and training harder before games expected to be wins is judgment, not tested [19:39].
- Resource context: he notes LSU gives him every resource. [04:11]
- Caption garbles around "coach time him off" at [05:12] (head strength coach, name unverified).

## Q&A

- Other sports? Five other sports use the weight room and the technology, including volleyball, baseball, women's soccer and beach volleyball; volleyball is trained like football. [22:17], [22:48]
- Screening before loading? Freshmen start in their own group, teach technique first, and go through screening with the medical staff before loading. [23:50], [24:21]
- Gap between regular season and bowl season? Force plate data guided adding strength work during the long break, then returned to the normal approach near competition. [24:52], [25:23]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: oZsFyPGij0U
title: "SSAC20: Playing Catchup: Estimating Player & Positional Value in (American) Football"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Paul Sabin]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

An ESPN analytics specialist presents a plus-minus style model that estimates a single season-level value for every football player. Plain plus-minus fails in football because players share the field nearly all the time, so the model gives each position its own variance, pulls low-snap players toward a prior based on draft rank, recruiting data or last season, and uses a heavy-tailed distribution. Results rank quarterbacks highest and put centers second in importance, which the speaker finds surprising. He shows checks (quarterback versus line, transfers) and lists planned changes. The talk gives no outcome validation beyond these plausibility checks.

## Key claims

- Football has lacked a single stat that values players across all positions, jumping from passer rating to tracking data. [03:42], [04:13]
- A standard plus-minus approach applied to 2018 college data put the top quarterback first and three offensive linemen next, which the speaker calls useless. [08:17]
- Players on the same unit were on the field together about 98 to 99 percent of plays, so the model cannot separate them without extra structure. [08:49]
- The fix: give each position a different variance, where higher variance means greater impact. [09:19]
- Low-snap players are not assumed average; the model shrinks them toward a prior from draft rank, recruiting data or the previous season. [09:49], [10:21]
- Players who play multiple positions get a weighted average across positions by snap share. [11:24]
- A heavy-tailed distribution lets the best players sit further from average. [11:54]
- In college data for 2019, quarterback variance is by far the highest and the center is second. [13:26]
- The speaker explains the center result by the center's role in calling blocking schemes, which film may not show. [13:56], [14:27]
- Tight end here means a player with a hand on the ground; a standing slot player counts as slot receiver. [14:27], [14:57]
- The position ordering is stable across NFL seasons since 2007, with running backs showing a lot of uncertainty. [14:57], [15:28], [15:58]
- The model rated Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson as the top players in recent NFL seasons and Derrick Henry as roughly top ten in impact. [15:58]
- The model's weakness: a strong passer on a run-heavy team may be undervalued (Russell Wilson example). [16:28]
- The previous-year prior held Joe Burrow back despite his strong season (caption: "Joe burrowed"). [17:30]
- Quarterback and line values are correlated but not tightly, so the model can separate them. [18:03], [18:34]
- Transfers in college improved on average; NFL movers declined on average. [19:05], [19:35]
- Inputs are position, on-field status, and down, distance and yard line for expected points. [20:05]

## Numbers and definitions

- About 70 offensive plays per team per game, so about 140 outcomes. [05:44]
- A college team plays about 12 of about 130 teams, described as around 10 percent (captions are muddled between "under" and "over" 10 percent). [06:16]
- Same-unit players on the field together: 98 to 99 percent of plays. [08:49]
- Student-t distribution with eight degrees of freedom, chosen for speed and thick tails, with no special justification. [11:54]
- Ridge regression parameter described as a ratio of model variance to prior variance. [07:46]
- Position scale parameter S_J, a variance multiplier by position. [09:19]
- Tight-end position is defined by alignment, not label. [14:27]
- NFL position distribution shown as a 90 percent interval. [27:15]
- NFL run: after each game window so values are ready next morning; college is slower due to manual tracking. [12:25]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Bayesian ridge-style plus-minus model fit in Stan. [12:25]
- Comparison with real plus-minus at ESPN, and a box-score prior in the planned descriptive version. [20:35], [21:06]
- Other metrics named: WAR, win shares, win probability added, Raptor, expected possession value, approximate value, an NFL scraper package, and a PFF WAR based on scout grades. [01:38], [02:10], [02:40]
- Boss named as Brian McDonald (caption). [02:10]

## Limits and open questions

- No out-of-sample test of player or position value is shown; checks are plausibility (transfer direction, quarterback versus line correlation).
- The center result is partly explained by hypothesis and the speaker admits the cause is open. [23:39]
- The caption name "Bobby Evans" at [08:17] looks wrong (caption spelling); not corrected.
- Model is built only on position, on-field status and expected points. [20:05] This excludes assignments, scheme and coaching.
- Planned changes show current gaps: separate run and pass models, predictive and descriptive versions, expected turnover points. [16:28], [20:35]
- Position importance is a posterior over variance; one questioner found the ordering unclear and the speaker clarified that these are distributions on variance. [26:45], [27:15]
- Institutional view: the author works at ESPN and frames the model for fans and storytelling. [00:37]

## Q&A

- Why does the model value centers more than draft position does? Mental and scheme-calling impact, seen in backups doing worse. [21:39], [22:09]
- Is it continuity? Part of it, but the effect differs for centers than other positions, still to be studied. [23:09], [23:39]
- Should coaches be included? Possibly, especially for judging how a player transfers to a new team. [24:09]
- Do center ratings track team success? Yes, less strongly; the top-rated center going into 2019 was Clemson's. [24:42]
- Why slot cornerbacks high? The speaker does not know. [25:13]
- Outside linebackers versus defensive ends? Position is by alignment, with a weighted average for those who play both. [25:43], [26:15]
- Why only college distribution shown? NFL was shown in a different format with a 90 percent interval. [27:15]

=== FILE: videos/2020-03-17_otCKz1OBpTg_instant-feedback-using-real-time-data-to-improve-training-ca/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: otCKz1OBpTg
title: "SSAC20: Instant Feedback: Using Real-time Data to Improve Training, Case Studies from MIT Sports Lab"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Kristina Chase]
topics: [sports-science, other-sport:track-and-field, other-sport:esports]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The managing director of the MIT Sports Lab argues that training data is often captured and processed but rarely returned to the athlete fast enough to help. She presents two case studies. For the US Olympic Committee, the lab used open-source pose estimation to find the takeoff frame and launch angle and velocity in long jump video, replacing hand tagging. For Red Bull high performance in esports, it tested whether automatically adjusting game speed with finer steps raised skill acquisition. Both are short project descriptions with few reported numbers. Her closing view is that analytics is a tool whose use depends on a defined question.

## Key claims

- Training is a loop of capture, processing, coaching and repeat, and much of what is captured is not put back into the immediate loop. [02:40], [03:43]
- In long jump, high-speed video is tagged by hand to find launch angle and velocity, and the USOC does not allow putting devices on athletes. [04:46]
- The result must return during the session, not an hour later. [04:46]
- The team used open-source pose estimation, which labels each frame separately, so raw output had to be processed to track the jumper. [08:31], [09:01]
- Detecting takeoff by the last point to leave the ground (the left toe in the example) reached about 99 percent accuracy, with small errors left. [09:32]
- Red Bull chose esports because every click is recorded. [10:33]
- Prior MIT research (Stephanie Muller, CSAIL, caption spelling) showed adaptive inputs can raise skill acquisition rate. [10:33]
- Experts gained most under the granular adaptive condition; at 10 percent adaptive most people did worse, since the change was too subtle to notice. [13:10]
- People are poor at judging when to make practice harder or easier, which automation can do. [13:40]
- Coaches filter what athletes hear, and a tool should give only what the coach asks for, such as launch angle and the exact frame. [20:35], [21:06]
- Analytics is a tool, not an answer; define the question and the action first. [21:36], [22:06]
- Passive collection with nothing on the athlete is where she sees the future. [23:06]

## Numbers and definitions

- Body locations tagged per frame: 19. [06:22]
- Frames for the jumping motion: "50 200" in the captions (garbled, likely 50 to 200). [06:22]
- About 2,000 points per frame by hand, as captioned. [06:52] This appears to conflict with 19 points and 50 to 200 frames; the likely meaning is per jump, but the captions say per frame.
- Pose tool identified eleven people in one frame, one being the jumper. [08:31]
- Accuracy reached: about 99 percent. [09:32]
- Adaptive rule: speed up 10 percent after a session of seven tries at 60 percent success; no change between 40 and 60; slow down below 40 percent. [11:37], [12:10]
- Granular rule: larger steps both ways, with a 30 percent slowdown if the athlete struggles. [12:40] The captions here are garbled ("forty to sixty", "twenty it's a hundred percent"), so exact step sizes are unclear.
- Task: a specific move in Super Smash Brothers (caption: "the wave -", probably a wave dash). [11:37]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Feedback loop: capture, process, coach, retry. [02:40]
- Open-source pose estimation with a custom algorithm to find the largest signal and reduce error. [09:01], [09:32]
- Control, adaptive and granular groups, with beginner, intermediate and expert players. [11:37], [12:40]

## Limits and open questions

- No sample sizes or statistics for the esports study, and the figure is described only by marker shape. [14:13]
- The jump accuracy figure of 99 percent has no sample size and applies to takeoff detection.
- The speaker says none of them expected the expert result. [14:13]
- Esports results come from a game, not a physical task.
- Several numbers are garbled in captions (see above).
- Host names and the speaker's lab role come from the introduction. The speaker also teaches at MIT. [01:03]

## Q&A
